pages.p:
A **loop** repeats code again and again. The simplest loop is **while**. After «while» you write a condition in round brackets, just like with «if».

The code in the braces runs, then JavaScript checks the condition again. It keeps going until the condition is false. One run of the braces is called a **round**.
pages.tip: «count++» adds 1 to «count». It is the same as «count = count + 1».

pages.p:
The loop stops only when its condition becomes false. So something inside the braces must change the variable that the condition looks at.

If nothing changes, the condition stays true forever. That is an **infinite loop**, and your program gets stuck. Here the countdown goes down each round with «n--», so it ends.
pages.tip: Before you run a while loop, ask: what makes this condition false in the end?

pages.h: for: a loop with a counter
pages.p:
Counting loops are so common that JavaScript has a shorter form: **for**. Its brackets have three parts, separated by semicolons:

• **start**: «let i = 1» creates the counter
• **condition**: «i <= 5» keep going while this is true
• **step**: «i++» runs after every round
pages.tip: The name «i» is just a habit (it means index). You can use another name.

pages.p:
You can start anywhere and step by any amount. To go down, use «--» or «-=». The condition decides when to stop.

The counter made with «let» exists only inside the loop. After the loop it is gone, and using it gives a «ReferenceError».
pages.tip: After 1 the counter would be -2. That is not above 0, so the loop stops.

pages.p:
Sometimes you want to leave a loop early. The word **break** ends the loop at once. JavaScript jumps to the first line after the loop.

Here we print numbers until their square is bigger than 30.
pages.tip: 6 times 6 is 36, which is more than 30. So «break» runs when «i» is 6.

pages.p:
The word **continue** skips the rest of the current round and goes straight to the next one. The loop does not end.

This loop prints all numbers from 1 to 5, except 3.
pages.tip: «break» leaves the whole loop. «continue» only leaves this round.

pages.p:
You can put a loop inside another loop. This is called **nesting**. For each round of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all its rounds from the beginning.

Think of a clock: for each hour, the minutes go around fully.
pages.tip: Use different names for the counters: «row» and «col», or «i» and «j».

pages.h: How many times does it run?
pages.p:
With nested loops, the inner body runs **outer rounds × inner rounds** times. Above, 3 rows and 2 columns give 3 × 2 = 6 lines.

The inner counter starts again each time the outer loop moves on. You can even use the outer counter in the inner condition.
pages.tip: When «i» is 2, the inner loop counts only up to 2.

pages.p: A very common job: add many numbers into one **total**. Make a variable before the loop, start it at 0, and add to it in every round. A variable that collects a result like this is often called an **accumulator**.
pages.tip: Make the accumulator **before** the loop. If you make it inside, it starts again every round.

pages.p: To count how many numbers pass a test, use a counter that starts at 0. Put an «if» inside the loop, and add 1 only when the test is true.
pages.tip: The numbers 3, 6 and 9 can be divided by 3 with no remainder. So the answer is 3.

pages.p: You can also collect text. Start with an empty string «""» and join something to it in each round with «+=». Nested loops make shapes: the inner loop builds one line, then you print it.
pages.tip: «stars» is made inside the outer loop, so every row starts with empty text.

pages.p:
When a loop confuses you, draw a table. Write one row per round and follow every variable. Here we multiply: the start value must be **1**, because 0 times anything is 0.

**i=1**: result 1 · **i=2**: result 2 · **i=3**: result 6 · **i=4**: result 24
pages.tip: Total starts at 0 (for adding). Product starts at 1 (for multiplying).

hand.why: The counter starts at 0 and the loop stops before it reaches 3, so it prints 0, 1 and 2.

hand.q:
How many times does the body of this loop run?
for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i++)
hand.why: The counter is 1, 2, 3 and 4. All of them satisfy «i <= 4», so the body runs 4 times.

hand.q: Complete the countdown so it ends.
hand.why: Something must make «n > 0» false in the end. Taking 1 off each round does that.
The loop adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, which is 10. Multiplying would give 24.

hand.q: What does the word «break» do inside a loop?
hand.ans: It ends the whole loop at once
wrong: It skips only the current round
It starts the loop again from the beginning
hand.why: «break» jumps out of the loop. The program carries on with the line after the loop.
For even numbers, «continue» skips the print. Only the odd numbers 1, 3 and 5 are shown.

hand.q: Complete the condition so the loop prints 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
hand.why: The loop must keep going while «i» is still 4 or less, which means the same as less than 5.

hand.q: Put the lines in order to make a countdown that ends with Liftoff.
hand.why: Make the variable first, then the loop that prints and changes it. «Liftoff» goes after the closing brace, so it prints once at the end.
Because «s» is text, «+=» joins instead of adding. The text grows: "1", "12", "123", "1234".
The outer loop runs 3 times and the inner loop runs 2 times each time, so «count++» runs 3 × 2 = 6 times.

hand.q: You want to keep halving a number until it is smaller than 1. You do not know how many rounds it will take. Which loop fits best?
hand.why: When you do not know the number of rounds, a «while» loop with a condition is the natural choice. «if» runs only once.

hand.q: A student writes: let i = 0; while (i < 3) { console.log(i); } — what happens?
hand.ans: It prints 0 again and again without stopping
hand.why: Nothing changes «i», so «i < 3» is always true. This is an infinite loop. Adding «i++» in the braces fixes it.

hand.q: Complete the line so the program prints hahaha.
hand.why: Each round joins the text «ha» to «word». After 3 rounds the text is hahaha.
«i» goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Since 16 is still 20 or less, it doubles once more to 32. Then the loop stops.

hard.why: The inner loop adds the numbers 1 up to «row» as text. Row 1 gives 1, row 2 gives 12, row 3 gives 123.
Even numbers are skipped. The odd numbers 1, 3, 5 and 7 are added (16). At 9, «break» ends the loop before adding. Without «break» the sum would be 25.
The counter goes 5, 3, 1. Next would be -1, which fails «i >= 1», so the loop ends.
«n» goes 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is 8 changes, so «steps» is 8.
Odd numbers are joined as digits, even numbers as a dash. The text builds up as 1, 1-, 1-3, 1-3-, 1-3-5.

hard.q: Which loop prints 1, 2 and 3 and then stops?
hard.why: This one starts at 1 and includes 3. The first prints only 1 and 2, the second prints 0 to 2, and the last one counts upward from 3 and never stops.
The inner loop runs 1, 2, 3 and 4 times. 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. A full 4 × 4 square would be 16, but the inner limit grows with «i».

hard.q: Complete the condition so the program counts the multiples of 5 from 1 to 20 and prints 4.
hard.why: A multiple of 5 leaves remainder 0 when divided by 5. The numbers are 5, 10, 15 and 20.

hard.q: Put the lines in order. The program should print 24.
hard.why: The product starts at 1 before the loop. The loop multiplies by 2, 3 and 4, and the print comes after the closing brace.

hard.q: After this code runs, what does the last line do?
hard.ans: It stops with ReferenceError: i is not defined
hard.why: A counter made with «let» in the for header exists only inside the loop. Outside it, the name is unknown.

items.symptom: It prints 5 but the total of 1 to 5 should be 15.
items.why: «total = i» replaces the total in every round. «total += i» adds to it.

items.symptom: It should print 1 to 5 and then Done, but 5 is missing.
items.why: «i < 5» stops before 5. Use «i <= 5» to include the last number.

items.symptom: It should skip only the number 3 (1, 2, 4, 5) but it prints just 1 and 2.
items.why: «break» ends the whole loop. «continue» skips only this round.
Anything times 0 is 0. A product must start at 1.

items.symptom: It prints one star, but it should print four: ****.
items.why: «=» replaces the text every round. «+=» adds a new star to the text.

items.symptom: It should count the multiples of 3 up to 10 (3), but it prints 4.
items.why: A multiple of 3 has remainder 0, not 1. The remainder 1 matches 1, 4, 7 and 10.

project.title: FizzBuzz Line
project.brief:
Write a function «fizzBuzz(n)» that returns one string with the numbers from 1 to «n», separated by single spaces. But:

• a multiple of 3 becomes «Fizz»
• a multiple of 5 becomes «Buzz»
• a multiple of both 3 and 5 becomes «FizzBuzz»

Example: «fizzBuzz(5)» returns «"1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz"». There is no space at the start or end. If «n» is 0, return an empty string.

tests.label: fizzBuzz(15)
tests.want: 1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz
